Bajo sexto 屬弦鳴樂器，歷史文獻有限，起源帶有歐洲影響。十九世紀中後期: The bajo sexto is a chordophone on which the historical literature is limited, and its origin carries European influence. In the mid and late nineteenth century a German music-shop chain set up in Mexico, and the accordion and the waltz and polka repertoire that immigrants brought were taken up locally; the duet of accordion and bajo sexto became an important form of northern music. Mexican makers had already built instruments with several courses of paired strings in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries; making flourished in the centre and south in the nineteenth, and the instrument moved north at the end of that century, used at weddings and at gift dances. Ensemble music arose in the 1930s, the double bass joined at the end of the 1940s and drums in the 1950s, which turned the bajo sexto towards a harmonic and melodic role.

低音六弦琴屬弦鳴樂器，以十二條弦成六組雙弦發聲，音域較一般吉他低八度；讀高音譜號: The bajo sexto is a chordophone that sounds twelve strings in six double courses, an octave below an ordinary guitar; read in the treble clef its actual pitch is a further two octaves down, so a written middle C sounds as C2. The older bass role was mostly played with the fingers, while modern chord and melody playing often uses a pick, and by that means the volume and the way the instrument speaks can change. The body is deeper, the neck shorter and the strings heavier, its low-frequency resonance is less than ideal, and some instruments have a pickup inside the soundhole to amplify the bass. Beside guitars of the same family it sounds in double courses and at a lower pitch; beside the bajo quinto it keeps the lowest course.
低音六弦琴常見於墨西哥地區音樂，早期以手風琴與小提琴為主的二人編制中擔任低音與節: The bajo sexto is common in the regional music of Mexico. In the early duets led by accordion and violin it took the bass and the rhythm, which let the accordion play more elaborate melodies. It also appears at weddings and at bailes de regalos (gift dances), often in ensemble with small drums. In conjunto and norteño it first supported the accordion with a plucked bass; once double bass, electric bass and drums were added it turned to playing chords, counter-rhythms and melodic lines. Its sound travelled with conjunto into Texas, where it is used in Tejano and similar line-ups.

The bajo sexto is a Mexican string instrument of the guitar family, Hornbostel–Sachs number 321.322-5. It has twelve strings in six double courses, a deeper body and a shorter neck. It is played much like a guitar: the left hand stops the strings at the frets to change the pitch, and the right hand plucks and strums with the fingers or a pick. It was originally designed to accompany accordion and violin players, and it is common in Mexican regional music, norteño and conjunto, and at weddings and dances.

When it takes the traditional bass role the fingers are mostly used to pluck; modern chord and melody styles often use a pick. A beginner can first learn the stopping positions of the six courses and practise the traditional tuning — the lower three courses in octave pairs, the upper three in unison pairs — then begin with simple plucking and strumming and gradually add melodic lines.
